newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Swaziland sees 495,000 tonnes 1997/98 sugar crop.
newsitem.headline: Swaziland sees 495,000 tonnes 1997/98 sugar crop.

text.p: Swaziland expects a 1997/98 sugar crop of 495,000 tonnes, up from the previous season's 471,000, the Swaziland Sugar Association said on Wednesday.
But Andy Colhoun, the association's general manager, said the forecast could be reduced by the effects of a five-week strike in February that might have led to some crop damage.

"The projected production for the 1997/98 season is 495,000 tonnes but this could be easily reduced by the effects of the five weeks stay-away which took place in February 1997," Colhoun told Reuters.
He said Swazi sugar production is projected to grow slowly over the next five years to reach around 540,000 tonnes in 2001/2002.
Production growth after that would depend on progress on two reservoirs.
Colhoun said the Maguga dam in the north-east was in early stages at present while the second reservoir -- planned for the south-east -- was not on the drawing board yet.
He said if the two dams were completed, some 20,000 hectares more land would be brought under irrigation, of which between 12,000 and 15,000 would be used for sugar.
Currently, Swaziland has 38,000 hectares under cane.
Colhoun said a South African press report on Wednesday saying Swaziland could triple its sugar production in the next five years was wrong.
"The claim that we could triple our production of sugar over the next few year is absurd," he said.
